title: India Rebuts Pakistan at UN: J&K and Ladakh Are Integral, Says Envoy
excerpt: First Secretary Petal Gahlot used India's Right of Reply at the 81st UN General Assembly to reject Shehbaz Sharif's remarks on Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty, accusing Pakistan of cross-border terrorism.
body:
• India's First Secretary to the United Nations, Petal Gahlot, used the Right of Reply at the 81st UN General Assembly on September 26 to rebut Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's address a day earlier.
  • Gahlot declared Jammu and Kashmir, including Ladakh, "an integral and inalienable part" of India, then turned the spotlight on Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, citing "wanton killings" and the denial of basic rights in Rawalakot.
  • She rejected Sharif's claim that India had "no legal basis" for holding the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, a step New Delhi took after the Pahalgam attack and Operation Sindoor in May 2025.
  • What to watch: Sharif warned that any Indian move to restrict Pakistan's share of Indus waters would be treated as "an act of war"; no bilateral talks are currently scheduled between the two countries.

India delivered a sharp rebuttal to Pakistan at the United Nations on Friday, exercising its Right of Reply at the 81st General Assembly session in New York to reject Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's remarks on Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty. First Secretary Petal Gahlot, speaking for India's Permanent Mission, accused Islamabad of using the world body to repeat familiar false claims while carrying out terrorism "at night."

The exchange followed Sharif's September 25 address, in which he raised the Kashmir dispute, defended Pakistan's conduct during the May 2025 military confrontation, credited Donald Trump with helping prevent escalation, and demanded a UN-supervised plebiscite in Kashmir.

"They claim to uphold security during the day; they actually carry out terrorism at night."

— Petal Gahlot, First Secretary, India's Permanent Mission to the United Nations

Context & Background

Sharif told the General Assembly that India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance had "no legal basis" and that any attempt to restrict Pakistan's water share would be treated as an act of war. On Kashmir, he said generations of Kashmiris had "waited for the United Nations to fulfil its solemn commitment to a free and impartial plebiscite."

Gahlot's response targeted each claim in turn. On Kashmir, she reaffirmed New Delhi's position and reversed the argument toward Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir: "References were made to the Indian Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir. This is an integral and inalienable part of my country and will always remain so. But if we must talk about Kashmir, let us turn our attention to the Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. Ask the people of Rawalkot about the wanton killings, the brutal violence and the denial of basic rights that they have long experienced."

India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty after the April 2025 terror attack in Pahalgam that killed 26 civilians, followed by Operation Sindoor, the cross-border military operation New Delhi launched in May 2025. Pakistan has rejected Indian allegations that it sponsors cross-border terrorism.

"References were made to the Indian Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir. This is an integral and inalienable part of my country and will always remain so."

— Petal Gahlot, First Secretary, India's Permanent Mission to the United Nations

Impact & Analysis

New Delhi's strategy at this session was to refuse internationalization of Kashmir and instead force the debate onto Pakistan's own record. Gahlot challenged Sharif's remarks on religious tolerance by pointing to Pakistan's blasphemy laws, and questioned the country's democratic credentials — calling it "a regime of the army, by the army, and for the army" and citing the 27th Amendment and the immunity granted to what she called Pakistan's "real ruler."

Invoking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, she noted that Osama bin Laden had been found in Abbottabad, close to a major seat of the Pakistani military — a reminder aimed at undercutting Islamabad's claim to stand against terrorism.

The sharpest escalation risk sits with the Indus Waters Treaty, whose suspension has frozen six decades of data-sharing and consultation mechanisms. Sharif's "act of war" framing raises the stakes of any Indian move on river flows, even as India maintains the suspension is a direct consequence of cross-border terrorism.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora — including the large Indian-American community — the exchange lands alongside the 25th anniversary of September 11, a reference Gahlot herself made on the UN floor. The Pahalgam attack that triggered the current standoff killed 26 civilians in Kashmir.

What's Next

The sparring has already moved to Geneva, where Pakistan used its Right of Reply at the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council this week to condemn India over Kashmir and minority rights. India is expected to answer in kind there as it did in New York.

The UNGA exchange changed little on the ground. Jammu and Kashmir remains under Indian administration, the Indus Waters Treaty remains in abeyance, and both countries continue to argue past each other — with terrorism, water, and sovereignty bundled into a single, hardening dispute.
